input.title: The Signal Tower: Seven Rooms of the Grid Machine
input.audienceRationale: The evidence sketches a nine-year-old who chose to talk about a wrestling state-championship loss, demanded harder riddles, spotted repeated riddles instantly, and called out faulty logic. That is not a child who wants sparkles for showing up — that is a child who respects a fair opponent and wants the difficulty to be honest. So the experience is framed as a machine that responds only to correct structure, never to enthusiasm. She gets to be the operator whose reasoning visibly powers something, because the evidence says she values being trusted with real difficulty and real hints on her own terms (she requested scaffolding when stuck rather than quitting). The reveal-based spelling activity feedback suggests staged reveals land well with children in this sample, so the world unlocks room by room — anticipation built by architecture, not confetti. Nothing here assumes a durable preference; it assumes a temperament: give her a worthy machine and get out of the way.
input.openingPromise: A tall, dark signal tower fills the right third of the screen, seven rooms stacked and unlit, with faint machinery silhouettes inside each. A single line appears: "This tower runs on equal groups. Nothing in it moves until the groups are right. Power it, room by room, and the top will send the signal." The promise is explicit and testable in the first minute: your math is the electricity. No mascot begs, no stars are offered. The tower simply waits, and one visible cable runs from the workspace on the left into Room 1.
input.firstThreeSeconds: Second 0–1: the tower fades in from black with a low hum, rooms dark, one amber pilot light blinking at Room 1 — a clear "start here." Second 1–2: the workspace on the left illuminates with four lunch trays already drawn, apple slices glowing softly inside them (item-01's full representation, exactly as authored). Second 2–3: the cable between workspace and tower pulses once, and the prompt text types itself in one quick line. Before three seconds are up the child can already see the whole causal chain: this picture, through this cable, feeds that tower. No menu, no title screen dwell, no instructions to read past.
input.firstAction: The very first interactive moment is Phase 0's orientation, staged as flipping the tower's master breaker: one large tap target. Flipping it plays the worked example — a voice-and-caption walkthrough naming "number of groups" and "amount in each group" over a sample display, with each phrase lighting the corresponding part of the picture. Nothing is assessed. Then item-01's four option tiles slide in as labeled fuse cartridges. Her first assessed action is tapping one cartridge and watching it slot into the cable junction. The tap target is huge (min 120px), works identically for touch and mouse, and there is no way to do it wrong mechanically — only mathematically.
input.interactionDemonstration: The breaker-flip orientation doubles as the interaction demo: when the sample display is narrated, the system visibly performs each gesture the session will use — a ghost hand taps a container to highlight it, drags one tile into an equation frame, and taps an option cartridge — each gesture labeled in three words or fewer ("tap to choose," "drag to build," "stretch to size"). This costs about twelve seconds and means every later mechanic (tap-select, tile-drag, corner-handle array sizing, tap-to-add tokens) has been seen once before it is ever required. The ghost hand never demonstrates on assessed content, only on the Phase 0 sample, so no answers are leaked.
input.coreInteraction: One loop, seven rooms, same grammar throughout: READ the situation on the left panel, BUILD or CHOOSE the mathematical structure (per each item's exact authored mode — single-select cartridges for items 01 and 04, tile-drag equation assembly for item-02, tap-to-create containers and tokens for item-03, corner-handle array sizing for items 05 and 06, free mode-choice construction for item-07), then SEND — a single commit button shaped like a lever. Pulling SEND routes the structure down the cable into the current room. If the structure is mathematically valid per the packet's validation rules, the room's machinery animates using the actual numbers: 4 trays of 3 become 4 gear clusters of 3 teeth engaging; 5 jars of 6 become 5 pistons firing 6 strokes each, counted aloud by the skip-count strip if she has revealed it. The commit lever is the heartbeat — deliberate, physical, hers. Nothing auto-submits; she always decides when her structure is ready to be judged.
input.mathAsPower: The mathematics is literally the power supply, and the mapping is exact, never decorative. The number of groups determines how many machine units spin up in the room; the amount in each group determines the size or stroke-count of each unit; the product determines the room's output wattage, displayed on an analog dial that sweeps to exactly that number. In item-05, both the 3×8 and 8×3 arrays drive the room's twin turbines to the identical 24-watt reading on two separate dials — the world itself demonstrates that the totals match while the arrangements differ, before she chooses her statement. In item-03, the unequal-groups display B, if routed, physically cannot mesh: the 5-token and 7-token gears grind against the 6-token ones and the room stays dark, showing why unequal groups fail rather than merely saying so. The product bank at items 05–07 stays physically disconnected (its cable visibly unplugged) until the construction validates, exactly as the upstream gating specifies. A wrong count anywhere means the machine stalls at the precise point of error — the fourth gear cluster with only 2 teeth visibly fails to engage — so the math's correctness is inspectable in the world, not asserted by a checkmark.
input.stakes: Each lit room feeds the one above it; the tower's signal at the top can only fire when all seven rooms hold power. The stakes are architectural and forward-looking, never punitive: the question is always "will the tower speak," and every room lit raises a visible voltage meter running up the tower's spine. At item-06 the stakes sharpen by her own hand — the harder tier is presented as an unmarked auxiliary room ("no picture this time; the grid starts empty"), and the framing is honest per the packet: declining costs nothing and closes nothing. The tension is anticipation of the top-floor signal, not fear of loss. Nothing she has already lit can ever go dark.
input.consequences: Consequences are diegetic and specific. A correct SEND: the room's machinery locks into rhythm, the wattage dial sweeps to the exact product, the room's window glows, and the feedback line (verbatim from each item's responseContract — e.g., "the first factor names how many jars; the second names how many buttons in one jar") appears etched on the room's brass plate. An incorrect SEND: the machinery attempts to run and stalls at the exact structural fault — wrong group count means missing gear clusters, wrong per-group amount means teeth that don't mesh — the dial drops back to zero, and the fault is described in groups language per the item's feedback contract. Distractor-specific consequences are honored: item-03's display B is named "not equal groups, so this cannot be an equal-groups model," never "close." No red X, no buzzer, no score deduction — the machine simply, legibly, does not run, and the reason is visible in the mechanism.
input.recovery: Recovery is dignified by design. After a stall, the workspace returns exactly as she left it — nothing is wiped, no attempt counter is displayed to her, and the room waits without commentary. Hints live behind a small wall-mounted intercom she taps herself, delivering the item's exact graduated hint ladder (restate → number of groups → amount in each group → partial representation), one rung per tap, never auto-triggered by wrong answers per the packet's hint policy. Given the evidence that this child requests hints when genuinely stuck and continues afterward, the intercom is visible but quiet — present, never pushy. Silent-struggle telemetry (consecutive misses without a hint request, idle-before-abandon time) is logged invisibly at every item as the packet requires, so the request-only policy can be evaluated without ever nagging her mid-session. Feedback never references speed, ability, or how many tries it took.
progression: Room 0 — Breaker: master-breaker flip plays the worked orientation with shared language and the ghost-hand gesture demo; nothing assessed.
Room 1 — Gear Floor (item-01): full picture given, tap one fuse cartridge; maximum support, the tower does the heavy lifting of showing cause and effect.

Room 2 — Piston Floor (item-02): picture still given but she must assemble the equation from tiles before the product; the optional skip-count strip appears as a pull-chain counter she reveals herself.
Room 3 — Foundry (item-03): direction reverses — equation given, representation built by her, with display B's grinding-gears rejection making the unequal-groups distractor physically legible.
Room 4 — Twin Panel Floor (item-04): equal-groups and array shown side by side driving the same 28-watt dial; the familiar form carries the new one, both panels fit without scrolling.
Room 5 — Turbine Floor (item-05): she sizes the array with a corner handle and live readout, then both arrangements run to matching 24-watt dials before she picks her statement.

Room 6 — Auxiliary Floor (item-06): her call — harder tier with a blank grid at 9×8, or standard tier with the partial 6×7 array; declining is acknowledged neutrally and the tower cares only that the room lights.
Room 7 — Signal Deck (item-07): blank workspace, her choice of builder, her equation, her product; every scaffold from below is gone and the whole tower waits on her unaided structure.
input.interactionContinuity: One physical grammar persists from Room 1 to Room 7: read left, build center, SEND right, watch the tower respond. Every new mechanic is an extension of an old one, never a replacement — tap-select (Room 1) becomes tile-drag into a frame (Room 2), becomes tap-to-create-and-fill (Room 3), becomes corner-handle stretch (Rooms 5–6), and Room 7 simply hands her the full toolbox she has already used piecemeal. The SEND lever, the cable, the wattage dial, the intercom, and the groups-and-amount language are identical in every room, so cognitive load stays on the mathematics, never on relearning the interface. The tower itself is the persistent continuity object: it is on screen from second zero to payoff, accumulating light.
input.worldReaction: The world reacts to structure, not to answers-as-tokens. Every validated construction is echoed back mechanically before judgment: when she builds 4 containers of 6, the room's intake visibly counts them — "4 containers... 6, 6, 6, 6" ticking on the intake gauge — mirroring the packet's requirement that container counts are reported back to the learner. Swapped factors in item-05 produce visibly different machine layouts (3 long turbines vs 8 short ones) with identical dials. Lit rooms keep faintly running for the rest of the session — their gears still turning at the pace her numbers set — so the tower becomes a living record of everything she has proven. Ambient details respond too: the tower's exterior lamps flicker up the spine as voltage climbs, and birds (or drones — visual team's call) begin circling the signal deck around Room 5, foreshadowing that something up there is waiting.
input.payoff: When Room 7 validates — her representation, her equation 7×5=35, her product, all mutually consistent — the SEND lever gets a heavier, two-stage pull. The tower draws all seven rooms' light up the spine in sequence (a two-second rising sweep, each room's product flashing on its dial as the charge passes), and the signal deck fires: a beam into the night sky that resolves into the full arc of her session — seven small constellations, one per room, each shaped like the structure she built (four trays, five jars, the 4×7 array, the twin turbines). The payoff line is the packet's own, spoken plainly: "You interpreted a situation, represented it, and matched it to an equation and its product." No generic praise, no comparison to anyone, no stars — the reward is that the machine she powered says exactly what she did, and the sky holds the proof. If she took the harder tier at Room 6, that constellation is simply drawn at 9×8 instead of 6×7 — the record is honest, not evaluative.
input.replayVariation: Replay keeps the academic packet immutable — same items, same answers, same difficulty, same sequence, per contract — while the world varies: room machinery re-skins (gears become water wheels, pistons become bellows), the ghost-hand demo is skippable after first completion, the tower's palette shifts (night/dawn/storm), and the final constellation sky accumulates across sessions so a second playthrough adds a second layer of stars rather than overwriting the first. The skip-count pull-chain, hint intercom, and tier choice remain live every time, so a replay can be a genuinely different strategic run (no hints, harder tier, array-mode-only at Room 7) of the identical mathematics. Variation lives entirely in surface and strategy, never in questions, answers, scope, or difficulty.
input.visualDirection: Warm industrial-mechanical, not grimdark: brass, amber glass, deep teal-navy backgrounds, so lit rooms genuinely glow against the dark. High-contrast token rendering — apple slices, buttons, seedlings, mugs, bolts, beads each get one saturated accent color against neutral containers so groups and amounts are separately countable at a glance, honoring every representationNote. Flat vector shapes with subtle grain, no photorealism, no visual noise near countable tokens. Layout is fixed for 1365×768 with zero scrolling: left 60% workspace, right 40% tower, dials and equation frames sized for touch (all targets ≥ 72px, primary targets ≥ 120px). Text is minimal, large, and typed-in rather than paragraph-dumped. Nothing on screen is decorative-only: every glow, dial, and cable is load-bearing meaning.
input.motionDirection: Motion is causal or it doesn't exist. Every animation traces the chain from her input to the world's response: tile slots with a settle, cable pulses travel workspace-to-room in ~400ms so cause and effect are never ambiguous, gears spin at rates proportional to the actual factors, dials sweep with slight overshoot-and-settle to their exact product. Stalls animate the fault, not a generic shake. The payoff sweep is the session's single longest animation at two seconds; everything else stays under 600ms so the machine feels responsive, not theatrical. No idle bouncing, no attention-begging wiggles on interactive elements — the blinking pilot light on the current room is the only "look here" cue, and it is diegetic. All motion respects prefers-reduced-motion with instant-state fallbacks.
input.soundDirection: A low ambient tower hum that rises almost imperceptibly in pitch as rooms light — the session's tension curve made audible. Interaction sounds are mechanical and specific: tile click-seat, lever thunk on SEND, gear-mesh ratchet on validated structures, a dull grind-and-wind-down on stalls (never a buzzer or sad trombone). Skip-count strip reveals tick audibly in rhythm — 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 — turning the counting strategy into something heard. Hint intercom opens with a soft radio crackle. The payoff beam gets the only melodic moment: a rising seven-note figure, one note per room. All narration captioned; full experience playable muted with no information loss; sounds short, dry, and never layered over each other.
usefulLibraries: pixi.js (performant 2D rendering for gears, tokens, dials at 60fps in-iframe)
gsap (timeline-based causal animation sequencing, cable pulses, dial sweeps)
interact.js (unified touch/mouse drag for tiles, corner handles, token placement)
zustand (small state store for room state, telemetry buffering, hint-ladder position)
input.engagementPrediction: Prediction: she completes all seven rooms in one session, opts into the harder tier at Room 6, and uses at most one hint rung at Rooms 3 or 7. Reasoning from evidence, not preference-projection: she requests harder challenges explicitly (harder-riddles evidence), she persists through multi-step problems when scaffolding is available on her terms (scaffold evidence), and she notices and rejects illogic (riddle-logic evidence) — which is precisely why the machine's failures are structurally honest; a child who catches faulty riddle logic will catch a game that lies about why an answer failed, and would disengage from it. The staged room-by-room reveal aligns with the positive small-sample feedback on the randomized-reveal activity. Predicted engagement risk points: Room 2's tile-drag if drag targets are fiddly on touch, and Room 6's tier prompt if the "harder" framing reads as a dare rather than an invitation — mitigated by neutral phrasing lifted directly from the packet.
input.falsifyingEvidence: This design is wrong if any of the following show up in telemetry or observation: (1) she declines the harder tier at Room 6 despite low hint usage and fast latencies beforehand — that would falsify the "worthy-opponent" framing and suggest the challenge invitation reads as pressure; (2) silent-struggle logs show consecutive misses with no intercom use followed by abandonment — the request-only hint policy is failing her and the intercom is too quiet; (3) opening_task_latency plus first-SEND time exceeds ~90 seconds — the tower metaphor is costing comprehension rather than buying motivation; (4) she reaches correct products at items 05–07 with representation_equation_consistency failures or elimination-pattern option tapping — the machine spectacle is rewarding outcomes over structure despite the gating, confirming the charter's selection-vs-construction concern; (5) she mutes or ignores the payoff and closes immediately — the earned-payoff thesis is wrong for this child and the reward economy needs rethinking; (6) transfer_task_unaided_success fails at Room 7 with heavy hint depth — per upstream, read this as a structure/sequencing signal for the packet, not as an experience failure, but it still falsifies the claim that the tower's continuity scaffolds independence.

decisionRecords.decision: Frame the entire session as powering a signal tower where the mathematics is literally the electricity; every factor, group, and product maps to a specific mechanical behavior.
decisionRecords.rationale: The contract demands the mathematics visibly control the world. A power metaphor makes the mapping exact and inspectable: groups = machine units, per-group amount = unit size, product = wattage dial. Nothing is decorative.
alternativesRejected: Narrative quest with characters (dialogue would dilute the causal chain and add reading load)
decisionRecords.risks: Metaphor comprehension cost at open; mitigated by the three-second causal reveal and breaker-flip orientation.

decisionRecords.decision: All assessed responses commit via one explicit SEND lever; nothing auto-submits.
decisionRecords.rationale: Preserves learner agency, prevents accidental touch submissions in a 1365×768 iframe, and makes every judgment moment deliberate — supporting dignified recovery because she controls when she is evaluated.
alternativesRejected: Auto-validate on placement (steals the decision moment, punishes exploration)
decisionRecords.risks: One extra tap per item; acceptable for the agency gained.

decisionRecords.decision: Wrong answers stall the machine at the exact point of structural fault, with the fault visible in the mechanism, never a generic error state.
decisionRecords.rationale: Evidence shows this child interrogates faulty logic; feedback must be as honest as she is. Also implements each item's feedback contract diegetically (e.g., item-03 display B's gears grinding).
alternativesRejected: Highlighting the correct answer (violates hint policy and product-never-first-hint rule)
decisionRecords.risks: Fault animations must be authored per distractor per item; scoped as the largest content-production line item.

decisionRecords.decision: Hints live behind a visible but quiet wall intercom, one graduated rung per tap, never auto-triggered.
decisionRecords.rationale: Implements the packet's learner-initiated graduated hint policy exactly, and matches the evidence that she requests scaffolding herself and continues afterward. Visibility without pushiness.
alternativesRejected: Proactive hint after N misses (violates packet policy)
Hidden hint menu (dignity of asking requires the ask to be easy)
decisionRecords.risks: If falsifier (2) fires, the intercom needs a single soft one-time affordance pulse, not a policy change.

decisionRecords.decision: Completed rooms keep running visibly for the whole session and can never go dark; the payoff constellation records the actual structures built, including the chosen tier at Room 6.
decisionRecords.rationale: Earned payoff requires an honest, accumulating record. Irreversible progress removes loss-fear so all tension is anticipation. Constellation-per-structure makes the payoff name the mathematics, per item-07's feedback contract.
alternativesRejected: Rooms dim on later errors (punitive, breaks recovery dignity)
decisionRecords.risks: Persistent animation cost; capped by rendering lit rooms at reduced tick rate.

decisionRecords.decision: Render the upstream gating (product bank locked until construction validates at items 05–07) as a physically unplugged cable that visibly connects only after validation.
decisionRecords.rationale: Honors the charter's selection-vs-elimination concern by making the gate legible rather than mysterious, and keeps the required instrumentation (selection-vs-construction accuracy gap) intact under the metaphor.
alternativesRejected: Greyed-out bank with no explanation (feels like a bug to a logic-sensitive child)

input.telemetryNotes: All recordedMeasures from every item's responseContract are buffered client-side and flushed per-room: opening task accuracy/latency, hint request counts and depth, skip-count strip usage, unequal-group distractor selection, factor-role assignment, representation-equation consistency, challenge opt-in rate, post-opt-in abandonment, transfer unaided success, completion rate, and the silent-struggle watch (consecutive misses without hint request, idle-before-abandon). Option-tap sequences at select items are logged to detect elimination patterns, feeding the charter's selection-vs-construction instrumentation requirement.
